common_name: Piedmont Ragwort (Yarrowleaf Ragwort, Blue Ridge Groundsel)

planting.note: Divide or plant container stock in spring into lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; Piedmont ragwort is a granite outcrop endemic and needs sharp drainage rather than the rich, moist woodland soil preferred by most Packera species.

directions: Packera millefolium is a granite outcrop endemic restricted to a handful of counties in the Blue Ridge and Piedmont of Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia, where it roots in thin, gravelly pockets of soil atop domes, cliffs, and rock outcrops fully exposed to sun. Unlike shade-loving relatives such as golden ragwort, it needs sharp drainage and should be planted in a crevice or rock garden with lean, mineral soil that dries between rains, since heavy clay or constant moisture will rot the crown. Its finely divided, almost fern-like basal leaves set it apart from every other Packera species, and clusters of bright yellow ragwort flowers appear on wiry stems in late spring above the foliage mat. It is ranked vulnerable by NatureServe due to its narrow range and specialized habitat, and it is not well suited to the hot, humid, high-rainfall summers of the Gulf Coast, where the shade-tolerant Packera species already in cultivation there are a better match.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification outdoors and germinates the following spring.

directions: Oregon bluebells is a Pacific Northwest woodland wildflower found from northern California through Oregon and Idaho into western Montana, where it grows in wet mountain meadows, seeps, and open, forb-rich clearings within conifer forests. Fresh seed should be sown in fall and left outdoors through a full winter of cold, moist stratification, since seed that is collected and stored dry germinates unevenly the following spring. Like its eastern relative Virginia bluebells, it produces nodding, bell-shaped flowers that open pink from the bud and age to blue, held above soft, hairy foliage on plants that die back to the ground by midsummer. It needs consistently moist soil and cool summer nights to perform well and is not a good candidate for the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate, where gardeners are better served by Mertensia virginica.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring and reset into consistently wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this species needs permanently saturated, boggy conditions and will not tolerate soil that dries out.

directions: Cuthbert's turtlehead is a rare wetland specialist known from a small number of sites in the Blue Ridge of North Carolina and Virginia and the Coastal Plain of Virginia, where it grows in sphagnum bogs, swamp-forest seeps, and other permanently saturated, acidic soils. Divide established clumps in early spring and reset them into constantly wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; because the species is so narrowly distributed and rarely propagated commercially, gardeners in most regions substitute the more available Chelone lyonii or C. glabra for a similar bog-garden effect. Compared to those relatives, it is a smaller, more compact plant with pink-purple flowers marked by a conspicuous yellow-bearded throat opening from late summer into fall. Its narrow range and habitat specificity make it a conservation-priority species best grown as part of regional native-plant restoration efforts rather than general garden use.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: Western Solomon's Plume (Western False Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this western subspecies spreads more robustly than the eastern subspecies and benefits from generous initial spacing.

directions: Western Solomon's plume is the Pacific Coast and Rocky Mountain counterpart to the eastern false Solomon's seal, ranging from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into California and east into the Rocky Mountain states, where it grows in moist, shaded mixed-conifer and hardwood forests up to mid-elevation. It is propagated almost exclusively by dividing dormant rhizomes in fall, since seed is slow and irregular to germinate; set divisions into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade. Botanically it is distinguished from the eastern subspecies by its more robust habit and leaves that clasp the stem directly without a short leaf stalk, and it bears the same plume-like clusters of small, fragrant white flowers in late spring that mature into red-speckled berries by late summer. It makes an excellent large-scale woodland groundcover across its wide native range, including warmer parts of coastal California, though it has not been widely tested as a garden plant in the true Gulf South.

planting.note: Divide established plants in spring and set into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this alpine and subalpine species needs cold winters and moist summers and does not tolerate heat.

directions: Alpine groundsel has one of the broadest ranges of any Packera species, occurring from Alaska south through the Cascades and Rocky Mountains to disjunct populations in California and Wyoming, with additional isolated stands in eastern Canada, always in cold, consistently moist habitats such as subalpine meadows, damp cliff faces, and open montane woodlands. Divide established plants in spring and set them into cool, humus-rich soil that stays moist through the growing season in partial shade to full sun, since it does not tolerate hot, dry summers. It forms a low rosette of rounded, toothed basal leaves and sends up short, leafy stems topped with clusters of yellow disk flowers that are rayless or bear only a few short rays, a distinctive trait that separates it from the showier, ray-flowered Packera species already common in cultivation. As a plant of cold alpine and subalpine climates, it is not a candidate for Gulf Coast gardens and is best appreciated in cold-climate native or rock gardens within its natural elevational range.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade; seed requires winter cold stratification outdoors and germinates the following spring.

directions: Prairie bluebells, also called foothill bluebells, is native to gravelly and sandy soils, streambanks, and open ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and aspen woodlands across the Rocky Mountain states and northern Great Plains, typically between about 5,000 and 12,000 feet elevation. Sow fresh seed in fall, direct into gritty, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded site, so it can experience the winter cold stratification it needs; established plants go summer-dormant like other members of the genus. It is shorter and more compact than woodland bluebells, with thicker, blue-green, glaucous leaves adapted to its drier native habitat, and its buds open pink before maturing into the same clear blue, bell-shaped flowers typical of the genus from April through June. Its need for a cold winter and dry summer dormancy make it poorly suited to the humid Gulf Coast, where it would be prone to summer rot, so it is best grown in cold-winter rock gardens or high-elevation native plantings within its natural range.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico
